A **distributional heatmap** shows a whole distributional data table at once.
As in a classical heatmap, rows are units and columns are variables, but each
cell is not a single colour: it is a horizontal strip split into segments
whose widths are the probabilities of the values and whose colours are the
positions of the values in the range of the variable. Each cell is thus a
"stacked bar" of the distribution, and a mostly green cell is a cell with
high values.

```{r}
library(DistrViz)
library(DDAWASS)

data(univer, package = "CUB")
univer$Faculty <- factor(sprintf("F%02d", univer$faculty))
univer$Gender  <- factor(univer$gender, levels = 0:1, labels = c("M", "W"))
items <- c("informat", "willingn", "officeho", "compete", "global")
M <- data2MatD(univer, unit = c("Faculty", "Gender"), vars = items,
               support = 1:7, min.n = 10)
dv <- dv_data(M, ranges = c(1, 7))
```

## The default heatmap

```{r}
hm <- dist_heatmap(dv)
hm
```

Rows and columns are reordered by two hierarchical clusterings, drawn as
dendrograms:

* **rows**: Ward's method (by default) on the L2 Wasserstein distance between
  the units, computed on all the variables (`DDAWASS::WD_hclust()` for
  discrete distributions, `HistDAWass::WH_hclust()` for histograms);
* **columns**: complete linkage on the distance $\sqrt{1 - r^2}$ between
  variables, where $r$ is the Wasserstein correlation
  (`DDAWASS::WD.correlation()`); with `col_dist = "1-r"` negatively correlated
  variables are kept apart.

The clustering results are stored in the `"clustering"` attribute of the plot
and can be used elsewhere, e.g. in a Green Eyes grid:

```{r}
cl <- attr(hm, "clustering")
cutree(cl$hc_rows, 3)
```

In the heatmap the cluster of faculties F06 and F13 stands out because of
the red and orange segments in all the columns, while the office hours
(`officeho`) are the aspect with the lowest ratings for most groups.

## Options

Clustering can be switched off for rows or columns, and the agglomeration
methods can be changed. The legend labels report the ends and the middle of
the range of the variables when it is common to all of them.

```{r, fig.height = 6}
dist_heatmap(dv, cluster_cols = FALSE, row_method = "average",
             palette = "RdYlGn", gap_y = 0.25, angle_x = 0)
```

With `cluster_cols = "tsp"` the columns are ordered by a short Hamiltonian
path through the variables (see `dv_var_order()`), which puts correlated
variables side by side without drawing a dendrogram:

```{r, fig.height = 6}
dist_heatmap(dv, cluster_cols = "tsp", col_dist = "sqrt(2(1-r))")
```

`style = "dark"` gives a black background, and the gaps between cells can be
controlled with `gap_x` and `gap_y`:

```{r, fig.height = 6}
dist_heatmap(dv, style = "dark", palette = "Zissou 1", gap_x = 0, gap_y = 0.05)
```

## Histogram data

For matrices of histograms the distributions are discretized into
`n_levels` equal-width classes. With `scheme = "standardized"` the colours
span $\pm 3$ Wasserstein standard deviations around the mean of each
variable, so that variables on different scales are comparable.

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
dist_heatmap(HistDAWass::BLOOD, n_levels = 20, scheme = "standardized",
             palette = "Zissou 1", style = "dark")
```

By default the clustering is computed on the original histograms
(`cluster_on = "source"`); with `cluster_on = "discretized"` it is computed on
the discretized distributions that are drawn.

## Interactive heatmaps

With `interactive = TRUE` (and the **plotly** package installed) the heatmap
is converted to an interactive plot: hovering over a segment shows the unit,
the variable, the value (or the class bounds for histograms), its probability
and the cumulative probability (not run here, to keep the vignette small).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
dist_heatmap(dv, interactive = TRUE)
```

## Reference

Irpino A., Verde R. (2015). Basic statistics for distributional symbolic
variables: a new metric-based approach. *Advances in Data Analysis and
Classification*, 9(2), 143-175. doi:10.1007/s11634-014-0176-4
